chunks: And from him, from Safwan, from Mu'awiya ibn 'Ammar, from Idris al-Qummi, who said:

I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): 'My slave performed Tamattu' (pilgrims who perform Umrah then Hajj). When he shaved his head, he put on his clothes before visiting the Kaaba. He said: 'What a bad thing he did.' I said: 'Is there anything wrong with him?' He said: 'No.' I said: 'For I saw Ibn Abi Sammak running between Safa and Marwah, wearing two socks, a qaba' (tunic), and a belt.' He said: 'What a bad thing he did.' I said: 'Is there anything wrong with him?' He said: 'No.' The way to reconcile these two narrations is to carry them upon being recommended (mustahabb) rather than obligatory (fard/wajib). That which indicates this is what he narrated.

key_terms.الصّفَا: Safa (one of the hills between which pilgrims walk)
key_terms.تَمَتّعَ: Tamattu' (a type of Hajj where one performs Umrah first, then Hajj)
key_terms.قَبَاءٌ: Qaba' (a type of tunic or upper garment)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on wearing clothes and socks after shaving the head during Hajj al-Tamattu'?
ai.summary: In this hadith from *Al-Istibsar*, Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies the juristic status of wearing clothes and footwear during the Ihram of Tamattu', resolving apparent contradictions by classifying these acts as *mustahabb* (recommended) rather than *fard* (obligatory) or *haram* (forbidden). This reflects the Shia scholarly principle of distinguishing between strict legal obligation and recommended practice, emphasizing ease in ritual observance. The narration underscores the flexibility within Shia fiqh regarding minor aspects of Hajr rituals, such as wearing socks and belts while performing Sa'i.
